summary: Presents a framework for large-scale measurement of broadband performance. It describes the logical architecture, the components and their interactions, and defines terminology for LMAP.

plainLanguage.summary: LMAP describes how one organization can coordinate broadband measurements across many devices. Controllers instruct measurement agents, and collectors receive the results, with security and privacy treated as core concerns.

subtitle: A framework for coordinating broadband measurements across large numbers of measurement agents.

tldr.problem: Large-scale broadband measurement needs a common way to coordinate tasks and collect results from many kinds of devices.
tldr.mechanism: Measurement Agents run tasks under Controller instructions and send Reports to Collectors using separate control and reporting channels.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines architecture and terminology, while leaving specific metrics, measurement methods, bootstrap mechanisms, and protocol choices to other work.

today: RFC 7594 is Informational. The work-unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the memo describes a framework and leaves specific protocols and metrics to other work.

sections.title: Goals and Main Components
sections.content:
The Large-Scale Measurement of Broadband Performance (LMAP) framework is intended to coordinate measurement tasks and collect results across a large population of Measurement Agents (MAs). Agents may run on PCs, consumer devices, home gateways, dedicated probes, or ISP network equipment. Use cases include network planning, fault identification, benchmarking, and diagnostics.

The three core components are the Measurement Agent, the Controller, and the Collector. The Controller instructs an agent what to measure and when; the Collector receives reports of the results. The framework aims for standardized, large-scale, diverse, and privacy-respecting systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Measurement agents perform tests or observe traffic. A controller schedules their work, and a collector receives their reports.

sections.title: Tasks, Instructions, and System Limits
sections.content:
A Measurement Method defines how to measure a Metric. A task can observe existing traffic or generate traffic for measurement. Generated tests may involve a Measurement Peer, which assists an agent but is not managed by the Controller. Instructions can include task configuration, schedules, report destinations, and suppression information.

The framework assumes one organization directs a Measurement System and each MA has one Controller at a time, though a system can have multiple Controllers. This avoids conflicting schedules on an agent. Bootstrapping provides an agent's identity, Controller information, and security details, but the RFC does not define a bootstrap protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: An instruction describes what to measure, when to do it, and where to send results. Each agent follows one controller at a time, so it does not have to resolve conflicting orders.

sections.title: Control, Measurement, and Reports
sections.content:
The Control Protocol delivers instructions from a Controller to an MA and can carry capability, failure, and logging information back. The MA then performs its assigned tasks without asking the Controller for permission before each one. A task may include a pre-check, such as confirming that the user is not already sending traffic.

The Report Protocol sends results and their context to a Collector. A report may include the agent or group identifier, result times, task details, a cycle identifier, or measurement-point designations. The transfer mechanism could use push, pull, multicast, or a hybrid approach; choosing and specifying the protocols is left to other work.

Suppression temporarily stops selected tasks or reports, for example during an unexpected network issue. It is not intended to permanently disable a task or an agent.
sections.plainLanguage: The agent follows its schedule, performs the measurement, and sends a report. A controller can temporarily suppress work when measurements or reports should pause.

sections.title: Deployment Choices
sections.content:
An MA may be installed on a networked device, embedded in a site gateway, placed behind a NAT or firewall, run on a multihomed device, or embedded in an ISP network. Placement affects which traffic it can observe and how a Controller can reach it. A site gateway can see site-to-ISP traffic, while an agent behind a NAT may need to initiate communications itself or use configured access.

A Measurement Peer may be a web server, a dedicated measurement endpoint, or another agent. Some tasks use two agents, one to send traffic and another to measure it. The Controller should account for agent capabilities and avoid measurement traffic that adversely affects users or their service.
sections.plainLanguage: The same measurement system can place agents in homes, devices, gateways, or an ISP network. Their location affects both what they can measure and how they communicate with the Controller.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Instructions must be authenticated, integrity-protected, and protected from replay. Reports must be encrypted, authenticated, and protected from tampering. Collectors should limit connections, transmission rates, and storage per agent to reduce resource-exhaustion risks. Results from customer-controlled devices may be untrustworthy, so operators should be cautious about using them for consequential decisions.

LMAP treats privacy as a core requirement. Measurement data can expose user identities, addresses, location, service details, traffic activity, or an ISP's measurement schedules and topology. The memo discusses minimizing collected data, aggregating general reports, using measurement-point names or group identifiers instead of direct identifiers, obtaining informed consent where appropriate, and limiting storage time.
sections.plainLanguage: Only trusted controllers should give instructions, and reports need protection from reading or alteration. Measurements can reveal private details, so collect and retain only what is needed and use identifiers that reduce exposure.
